result:
There's a sound my refrigerator makes at 3:17 in the morning.

I only know the exact time because I happened to be awake for it. I was standing in the kitchen in socks, drinking water straight from a glass that I hadn't bothered to put on a coaster or in the right place or anything, and I heard it. It wasn't the normal hum. It was a little click, then a shudder, then a sigh as the compressor decided to take a break. It's a sound that thing has made, I assume, twice an hour for the last eight years. And for eight years I have not heard it once. Not really heard it.

That's been on my mind for a few weeks now — not the refrigerator, but the category of things that the refrigerator belongs to. The things that work so well and so constantly that they become invisible.

We love to talk about creation. We have a whole mythology for it. Someone has an idea in the garage, in the shower, on a napkin at a bar. A spark. A eureka moment. They build the thing, they launch the thing, they disrupt the thing. We put those people on magazine covers. We give them TED Talks. Creation is sexy, dramatic, and it has a clear beginning, middle, and end.

Nobody puts maintenance on a magazine cover.

Maintenance doesn't have a eureka moment. Maintenance has a Tuesday. And then another Tuesday. And then another Tuesday after that, for about forty years.

I think we have fundamentally misunderstood what holds the world together. We think it's invention. It's not. It's maintenance.

Consider the building you are in right now. Somebody designed it, yes. An architect drew the lines, some developer found the money. That took maybe two years. But someone has mopped its floors every night since it opened. Someone replaced the burnt-out bulbs in the hallway. Someone unstuck the elevator doors in 2019 when they jammed. Someone cleaned the gutters before the storm. Someone re-caulked the windows. If they had stopped doing any of those things for even six months, the building would have started to rot, to stink, to fail. The building exists at all not because it was created, but because it is being continuously re-created, every single day, by people whose names are not on the plaque out front.

My grandfather fixed clocks. Not as a job — as a compulsion. He had a little workshop in his basement that smelled like oil and old wood and pennies. He had tweezers that looked like they belonged to a surgeon and these tiny little jars full of gears that would rattle if you shook them. When I was nine or ten, I would go down there and watch him work. He would have a clock disassembled across a felt mat — hundreds of pieces, springs coiled like sleeping snakes — and he would pick up each one with infinite patience. He never seemed to be in a hurry. 

I asked him once why he didn't just buy a new clock. Quartz clocks from the drugstore were ten dollars and were more accurate. He laughed, not in a mean way, but like I had said something genuinely strange.

"This clock," he said, and he pointed to a big, ugly, beautiful Regulator wall clock he had been working on for three weeks, "was built in 1898. It hung in a train station in Ohio. It told people when to go home. It survived two world wars and a flood. Someone just decided it was worth keeping on ticking. That's not about accuracy. That's about an agreement."

An agreement. I didn't understand what he meant then. I think I do now.

The agreement is: I will keep you existing. And in return, you will keep reminding me that time is passing.

Everything entropy touches requires this agreement. Everything. Your body is not a finished thing. Your body is a maintenance project you inherited without being asked. Every seven to ten years, almost every cell you have will have been replaced. Your skin is new this month. Your stomach lining is new every few days. You are not a statue; you are a fountain pattern that looks stable because water keeps running through it. You have to eat, sleep, stretch, drink water, go outside. If you stop, you end. Life is not an achievement. It is a practice.

This is true of houses and this is true of love and this is true of friendships and this is true of knowledge.

I used to think I was bad at friendship because I wasn't intense enough. Other people had these grand gestures — weekend trips, five-hour phone calls, matching tattoos. I didn't. I just... texted back. I remembered that your mom had surgery last week and asked how it went. I sent you a meme that reminded me of you. It felt small, almost embarrassing. It felt like maintenance, not creation.

And then I turned thirty, and I realized all my friendships that had survived were the maintenance friendships. The ones where someone kept choosing, in tiny increments, to not let the thing decay. The grand gesture friendships had burnt bright and then quietly died because nobody wanted to do the dishes afterward.

There's a concept in software that has stuck with me. Most people imagine software as being built: engineers hammer it out, release it version 1.0, done. But anyone who has ever worked on real software knows that 80% of the work is not building it. It's maintaining it. It's fixing the bug that only happens when a user with a name containing an apostrophe tries to check out on a leap year. It's updating the code because some other library that your code depends on updated theirs and now nothing talks to each other. It's answering the same question in the forums for the fourth year in a row.

The most important people in the open-source world are not the brilliant visionaries who started the projects. They are the maintainers. The tired, slightly annoyed, incredibly generous maintainers who have spent ten years saying, "No, you can't merge that, it breaks backward compatibility," at 11 p.m. on a Sunday. They are the reason the entire modern internet does not collapse tomorrow. Most of them are unpaid. Most of them are burned out. And without them, nothing works.

We have, culturally, zero respect for this.

We think of cleaning as what you do before something important happens. But cleaning IS what happens. The constant pushing back of dust, disorder, mold, and chaos is the actual work of living. The philosopher's house and the poet's house both need their toilets scrubbed.

Last year I started trying to notice maintenance workers on purpose. Not in a creepy way. Just to actually see them. The guy at the grocery store who was on his knees restocking yogurt at 6 a.m., putting the new expiration dates in the back. The woman at the park who picks up trash even though it's not her park, with a little grabber tool. The librarians who re-shelve books that children have pulled out and left in piles. The city crew that paints over graffiti before noon. The IT person at your job whose name you don't know who reset your password and kept the email server from being blacklisted again.

It's everywhere, once you look. It's like a secret second city, built on top of the first, made of people keeping the first city from drowning.

I think this is why we feel so weird about adulthood. When you're a kid, you think adulthood is creation — you'll build a career, build a family, build a house. Then you get there and find out that actually, adulthood is mostly maintenance. You have to keep the job, keep the house from falling apart, keep your teeth, keep your car running, keep your relationships, keep your own mind from slipping into the dark water. And no one ever framed it as noble. They framed it as drudgery. So you feel like you're failing because you're just... maintaining. When in fact maintaining is the most noble thing you can do.

My friend Lina takes care of her mother, who has Alzheimer's. She has done this for five years. She quit her job in graphic design to do it. When I visit, her mother sometimes knows her and sometimes thinks she's a stranger who has come to steal the silverware. Lina makes the same lunch, answers the same questions, cleans up. There is no progress. There will be no cure in time. There will be no thank you that will be remembered the next day. I used to not know what to say to her. I wanted to say something inspiring like "You're so strong" or "What you're doing is amazing." But that felt like creation language, and what she was doing wasn't creation language.

One day I just said to her, "Thank you for keeping her here. Thank you for keeping her safe and clean and comfortable while time does what it does." She started crying. She said, "That's exactly it. I'm just keeping her here."

That is holy work, I think. Keeping someone here.

Maybe that's what love is, ultimately. Not the fireworks at the beginning — though those are nice. But the quiet, stubborn, almost boring decision to keep something or someone existing past the point where it would naturally disappear. To wind the clock again. To defrost the freezer. To sweep the floor even though ten minutes after you sweep it, someone will walk across it with muddy shoes.

We are all on a spinning rock that is trying, constantly, to shake us off and freeze us and irradiate us and forget us. Entropy is the default. Disorder is the default. The refrigerator humming stops being invisible when you realize it's not a hum at all. It's a prayer. It's saying, over and over, "Not today. Not today will the milk spoil. Not today will the food rot. I am still here. I am still cold."

If you listen at 3:17 in the morning, you can hear everything else doing the same thing. The streetlights staying on. The hot water heater staying warm. The house settling but not collapsing. Your heart beating. Your lungs pulling in air and pushing it out without you having to remember how.

It's all maintenance. It's all someone — something — choosing to keep going.

Maybe, if we could learn to be proud of our maintenance, we would be happier. Maybe if we celebrated the people who keep things ticking instead of just the people who made them tick once a long time ago, we would have a gentler world. Maybe if we told our kids, "You are going to grow up and you are going to do a million small, invisible things that keep the world from falling apart, and that will be your life's great work," they would not feel so ashamed when they found themselves spending a Saturday morning fixing the toilet.

I didn't fix my refrigerator that night. It didn't need fixing. It just needed to be heard. I stood there and listened to its full cycle — click, shudder, hum, sigh — until it finished. It took maybe four minutes. And then the apartment was silent, except for my own breathing and the faint, far-away hiss of cars on the wet road outside, which were also being maintained by people I will never meet, who were filling potholes and repainting lines while I slept.

When it was done, I patted the top of the fridge, like it was a dog. Which is ridiculous. I know.

But it felt like an agreement.
